english.notes:
(i) From 13th November 2018, an aggravated version of this offence applies where the offence is committed against an emergency worker acting in the exercise of his / her functions as such a worker, as per section 1 of the Assaults on emergency Workers (Offences) Act 2018; see offence wording document H19568.
(ii) Practical Considerations - a brief resume:-
A battery is an intentional or reckless act whereby unlawful force is inflicted. A mere touch can amount to battery;
Where there is no injury, question whether the circumstances justify a charge at all;
Where injury is sustained, assess the degree/severity of injury before charging.
CPS guidelines specify that injuries of the following severity should normally be charged as battery:-
grazes, scratches, abrasions, minor bruising, swellings, reddening of the skin, superficial cuts and a "black eye".
There may be borderline cases, such as an undisplaced broken nose (cartilage displaced from bone).
Consider section 47, 20 or 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 for serious injuries.
(iii) This offence wording applies to common assault by beating (physical contact). See H4325 for assault by putting in fear of immediate violence, see also DPP v Taylor, DPP v Little (1992) 95 Crim App R 28.
(iv) See the charging standards relative to this charge heading.
(v) This is a summary offence only but see Sections 40 and 41 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988, Section 40 (allowing a common assault to go with indictable charges to Crown Court) applies to common assault, but not expressly to assault by beating. However in R v Lynsey 1995 the Court of Appeal stated that the term should be used in its widest possible sense and therefore common assault by beating could be used in an indictment with other charges under section 40. Under section 41 of the same Act the Crown Court have a general power to try certain summary offences including common assault, but the Lynsey case would appear to make this provision unnecessary for common assaults (of any type).

other.penalty:
Six months imprisonment and / or a fine not exceeding level five on the standard scale.

On the 12th March 2015 the limit on fines imposed by a Magistrates’ court was removed – as such, the potential fine on summary conviction in relation to an offence committed after this date is unlimited.

Time limit for prosecutions:
6 months

In domestic abuse cases committed on or after 28th June 2022 - see section 39A of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 regarding time limit.
